abstract: A common and effective strategy for humans to improve an unsatisfactory outcome in daily life is to find a cause of this outcome and correct the cause. In this paper, we investigate whether this human improvement strategy can be applied to improving reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for alignment of language models (LMs). In particular, it is observed in the literature that LMs tuned by RLHF can still output unsatisfactory responses. This paper proposes a method to improve the unsatisfactory responses by correcting their causes. Our method has two parts. The first part proposes a post-hoc explanation method to explain why an unsatisfactory response is generated to a prompt by identifying the training data that lead to this response. We formulate this problem as a constrained combinatorial optimization problem where the objective is to find a set of training data closest to this prompt-response pair in a feature representation space, and the constraint is that the prompt-response pair can be decomposed as a convex combination of this set of training data in the feature space. We propose an efficient iterative data selection algorithm to solve this problem. The second part proposes an unlearning method that improves unsatisfactory responses to some prompts by unlearning the training data that lead to these unsatisfactory responses and, meanwhile, does not significantly degrade satisfactory responses to other prompts. Experimental results demonstrate that our algorithm can improve RLHF.

title: Shortcut Features as Top Eigenfunctions of NTK: A Linear Neural Network Case and More
central_claim: Shortcut features in biased datasets are more aligned with the top eigenspaces/eigenfunctions of the NTK than ground-truth/core features, so they are learned faster and can dominate model outputs; this is shown theoretically for linear networks and empirically for ReLU networks/ResNet-18.
claim_evidence: The abstract states that shortcut features correspond to features with larger eigenvalues and remain influential after training, and that these properties are empirically extended to two-layer fully connected ReLU networks and ResNet-18. The main empirical support is Section 4/Experiments, especially Figure 5, which reports higher availability for shortcut labels than ground-truth labels on Waterbirds and CelebA, and Appendix Figure 8/Table 2, which reports the same for smaller synthetic Colored-MNIST and Patched-MNIST experiments.
mre_config: Cheapest valid MRE: reproduce the synthetic Patched-MNIST or Colored-MNIST availability experiment from Appendix C/Figure 8 using a two-layer ReLU fully connected network of width 256. Construct biased MNIST labels where digits 0-4 map to -1 and 5-9 to +1; add the shortcut feature to 95% of one class and 5% of the other in training, with a balanced 50/50 shortcut ratio in test. Train with SGD, learning rate 0.001, weight decay 0.0001, batch size 1000, for enough updates to measure early availability, using CE or MSE. Compute empirical NTK on 500 randomly sampled training points and compare availability A(K,g) for the shortcut label versus ground-truth label. Anchor metric: shortcut-label availability minus ground-truth-label availability should be positive at about the 1000th SGD update; Appendix Table 2 reports +0.0977 ± 0.0129 for Colored-MNIST CE and +0.0160 ± 0.0061 for Patched-MNIST CE. Tolerance: positive difference with magnitude within roughly one order of the reported value or clearly above zero across several random seeds.
agent_task: Implement the Patched-MNIST or Colored-MNIST construction from MNIST, train a width-256 two-layer ReLU fully connected network using the paper's optimizer settings, compute the empirical NTK on 500 sampled training points during training, and verify that the shortcut label has higher availability than the ground-truth label around the 1000th SGD update.

code_available.evidence: No OpenReview supplement was provided in the input, and the paper checklist says code/data are not yet released. Live web searches for the exact title, arXiv ID 2602.03066, OpenReview ID TYroQXu6X0, author names, and GitHub/code variants found the OpenReview/arXiv/NeurIPS paper pages but no public repository or runnable scripts for the Patched-MNIST/Colored-MNIST availability MRE.

dataset_available.evidence: The MRE can be built from MNIST, which is publicly available through torchvision.datasets.MNIST with a documented download parameter. The paper text specifies the MRE-specific biased construction: digits 0-4 labelled -1, digits 5-9 labelled +1, with a 95/5 shortcut ratio in training and 50/50 in test for Patched-MNIST/Colored-MNIST. No first-party processed split files were found, but the raw dataset and construction recipe are sufficient for this minimal derived benchmark.

weights_available.evidence: The MRE trains a small two-layer ReLU fully connected model from scratch and does not require pretrained weights. Searches for the title/arXiv ID plus checkpoint, weights, model, Hugging Face, and GitHub variants found no released checkpoints or model files for the MRE.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: MNIST itself is a standard public benchmark, verified via torchvision documentation, but the actual MRE dataset is an author-defined biased derivative, Patched-MNIST or Colored-MNIST, with custom shortcut features, custom binary labels, and custom train/test shortcut ratios. Therefore the MRE dataset is not a standard benchmark as used in the paper.

h100_estimate.basis: The appendix reports that experiments with synthetic datasets ran for about 1 hour on 2 RTX 3090 GPUs. The GPU normalization table does not list RTX 3090, so 0.15 H100-equivalent per RTX 3090 is used as an approximate FP16-class multiplier comparable to nearby listed non-datacenter GPUs. Arithmetic: 2 GPUs * 1 hour * 0.15 = 0.30 H100-hours. This counts only compute for the MRE; engineering time to recreate missing code is additional.

abstract: One of the chronic problems of deep-learning models is shortcut learning. In a case where the majority of training data are dominated by a certain feature, neural networks prefer to learn such a feature even if the feature is not generalizable outside the training set. Based on the framework of Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), we analyzed the case of linear neural networks to derive some important properties of shortcut learning. We defined a feature of a neural network as an eigenfunction of NTK. Then, we found that shortcut features correspond to features with larger eigenvalues when the shortcuts stem from the imbalanced number of samples in the clustered distribution. We also showed that the features with larger eigenvalues still have a large influence on the neural network output even after training, due to data variances in the clusters. Such a preference for certain features remains even when a margin of a neural network output is controlled, which shows that the max-margin bias is not the only major reason for shortcut learning. These properties of linear neural networks are empirically extended for more complex neural networks as a two-layer fully-connected ReLU network and a ResNet-18.

title: Learning to Solve Complex Problems via Dataset Decomposition
central_claim: Recursive dataset decomposition plus difficulty-based curriculum improves small language models' mathematical/code reasoning performance compared with standard supervised fine-tuning on the original datasets.
claim_evidence: The abstract states that the method recursively generates easier components and constructs curricula, and that experiments on MATH, AIME, and code generation show superior performance over standard training. The headline empirical evidence is Table 2/AIME2025: Qwen3-4B-Base fine-tuned on AIME2024 improves from SFT 3.3±3.3 to SFT-Decomp 13.3±6.3 and SFT-Decomp+Curriculum 16.7±6.9 using 385 decomposed examples; Table 1 similarly reports MATH-500 gains for Qwen2.5-1.5B.
mre_config: Cheapest valid MRE: reproduce the AIME experiment with Qwen3-4B-Base. Generate the decomposed training set from the 30 AIME2024 problems using the paper's recursive decomposition procedure with a GPT-4o teacher, train Qwen3-4B-Base for 5 epochs on the 385 decomposed examples under the stated SFT settings (batch size 16, bf16, AdamW, lr 1e-5, 5% warmup, cosine decay), optionally order examples by the paper's difficulty score for the curriculum variant, and evaluate greedy pass@1 accuracy on the 30 AIME2025 problems. Anchor metric: AIME2025 accuracy; a reasonable tolerance is matching the direction and rough magnitude of the reported gain over SFT, e.g. SFT-Decomp around 13.3% and curriculum around 16.7% within the large binomial/seed error bars.
agent_task: Implement the recursive dataset decomposition algorithm from the paper; obtain the 30 AIME2024 training problems and 30 AIME2025 test problems; use GPT-4o to split each AIME2024 CoT into steps, create tags and subquestions, solve and verify subanswers, recurse to the paper's depth/retry settings as inferable from the text, compute concept-graph difficulty scores, fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Base for 5 epochs on the resulting decomposed set, and evaluate greedy pass@1 on AIME2025 against the reported SFT-Decomp and curriculum accuracies.

The bundled OpenReview supplement manifest contains only 'Supplementary Material/Technical Appendices and Supplementary Material.pdf' and a macOS metadata file, not runnable training/decomposition/evaluation code.

dataset_available.evidence: The raw benchmark problems AIME2024/AIME2025 are public competition benchmarks, but the MRE depends on the paper-specific 385-example decomposed AIME2024 training set, with generated subproblems, CoTs, answers, tags, depths, and difficulty scores. Searches on the title, SFT-Decomp, AIME2024 decomposition, and Hugging Face-scoped variants did not find a released dataset. The OpenReview supplement manifest contains only PDF supplementary material, not the generated data files or construction scripts.

weights_available.evidence: Searches on Hugging Face and the web for Decomp/SFT-Decomp with Qwen3-4B-Base, AIME2024, Wanru Zhao, and dataset decomposition found no released fine-tuned checkpoints or adapters for the MRE. Public base models such as Qwen3-4B-Base do not count as the paper's MRE-relevant trained weights, and the OpenReview supplement manifest includes no model/checkpoint files.

dataset_is_standard.evidence: Although AIME itself is a widely used public math contest benchmark, the MRE training data is an author-created synthetic/decomposed derivative dataset with custom subproblems, tags, depths, and difficulty scores. Therefore the MRE dataset is not a standard off-the-shelf benchmark dataset.

h100_estimate.basis: The paper states experiments used NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs and gives training hyperparameters but does not report GPU count or wall-clock time for the MRE. The selected MRE is small: SFT of a 4B model for 5 epochs over 385 generated examples plus greedy evaluation on 30 AIME2025 questions. Ignoring the unavailable-artifact engineering burden and the external teacher-model data-generation cost, an order-of-magnitude estimate is about 1-3 H100-hours for fine-tuning/evaluation, reported as 2 H100-hours. Engineering/debugging time and paid API calls to regenerate the decomposed dataset are additional and not included.

abstract: Curriculum learning is a class of training strategies that organizes the data being exposed to a model by difficulty, gradually from simpler to more complex examples. This research explores a reverse curriculum generation approach that recursively decomposes complex datasets into simpler, more learnable components. We propose a teacher-student framework where the teacher is equipped with the ability to reason step-by-step, which is used to recursively generate easier versions of examples, enabling the student model to progressively master difficult tasks. We propose a novel scoring system to measure data difficulty based on its structural complexity and conceptual depth, allowing curriculum construction over decomposed data. Experiments on math datasets (MATH and AIME) and code generation datasets demonstrate that models trained with curricula generated by our approach exhibit superior performance compared to standard training on original datasets.
